Classic linear optimizers maximize expectation under independence, leading to over-exposure to high-variance, highly-correlated assets. This shifts the decision-making from a single-point estimate to a distribution over outcomes, enabling risk-aware lineup construction. It starts by visualizing pairwise correlations between a quarterback and receivers (Figure 4), establishing that stacking players from the same high-performing offense yields higher joint probability mass than pairing dissimilar roles. The 'Race' algorithm (Section 2.4) transforms these multivariate distributions into actionable portfolios by solving a constrained maximization problem for each Monte Carlo sample, effectively converting a predictive model into an optimizer. The empirical evaluation (Section 3) uses normalized z-scores to compare against two baselines: salary-cap random portfolios and knapsack-optimized portfolios without correlation. The key insight is that tournament winners often exploit co-movements (e.g., Watson-Johnson receiving combo in Week 14, 2019), which the knapsack baseline fails to capture due to its marginal optimization. The backtest results demonstrate that incorporating stacking correlations increases tournament Sharpe ratio by 61% relative to the salary benchmark and 57% relative to the knapsack baseline, confirming the thesis that correlation-aware optimization improves exposure to tail-event winners in large-field GPPs.
